cret-080.title: Antarctica, the land bridge between two continents
cret-080.text: Kangaroos have South American roots, and the route they took ran across Antarctica. In the Late Cretaceous and early Paleogene, Antarctica joined Australia and South America by land. Marsupials appear to have crossed from South America through Antarctica to reach Australia. Traffic ran both ways: platypus-like monotremes made the opposite trip, arriving in southern South America in the latest Cretaceous.

cret-082.title: The thylacocephalans, a crustacean riddle, disappear
cret-082.text: Some animals leave behind more questions than answers. Thylacocephala, an enigmatic class of crustaceans, is one of them. These shelled sea creatures, relatives of crabs and shrimp, puzzle researchers to this day. Their long story closed in the Late Cretaceous, when the last of the class went extinct, one quiet loss among the many changes reshaping the seas.

cret-083.title: Meridiolestidans, South America's forgotten mammal rulers
cret-083.text: Long before llamas or armadillos, South America's mammals belonged to a group few people have heard of. Meridiolestidans were the dominant mammals of the continent in the Late Cretaceous. They came in surprising variety, from the sabre-toothed Cronopio to plant-eating mesungulatids. The group also proved remarkably durable: it outlasted the age of dinosaurs and lingered in Patagonia until the Miocene.

cret-084.title: Shell-crushers perfect the Mesozoic marine revolution
cret-084.text: In Late Cretaceous seas, a shell was no longer a safe place to hide. Shell-crushing predation, the force behind the Mesozoic marine revolution, was perfected by marine reptiles and other hunters. Sea urchins joined in, radiating into predatory niches and probably perfecting the grazing of corals. Even the land may have fed the arms race: faster weathering and nutrients washing off from the boom in flowering plants may have helped drive it.

cret-087.title: The Mississippi embayment, cradle of a great delta
cret-087.text: The Mississippi River Delta has a surprisingly deep history. It traces back about 100 million years, to the Late Cretaceous, when a broad low trough called the Mississippi embayment formed. That embayment, an arm of lowland open to the sea, gave the future river a path to the Gulf. Everything the delta became later was built on this ancient foundation.

cret-088.title: Modern birds take flight in the Cretaceous
cret-088.text: Every duck, sparrow and ostrich alive today descends from birds that shared the world with dinosaurs. Modern birds, the Neornithes, probably arose around the boundary between the Early and Late Cretaceous, about 100 million years ago. Around then, their ancestors evolved a more open pelvis for laying larger eggs, and by about 95 million years ago they had a sharper sense of smell. A 2015 study placed their last common ancestor near 95 million years ago and the fowl–Neoaves split at 85. A 2024 genomic study pushed that split back to about 100.5 million years ago. The dating is contested, though: molecular clocks favor a Cretaceous radiation, while fossils point to a Paleogene one, a dispute called 'rocks versus clocks'. Only waterfowl and shorebirds have an established Late Cretaceous fossil record. The birds diversified dramatically around the K–Pg extinction.

cret-086.title: Spinosaurus and the giant hunters of North Africa
cret-086.text: Few places have ever held so many giant meat-eaters at once. In the mid-Cretaceous, North Africa was ruled by abelisauroids, spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids, found side by side in the Kem Kem, Bahariya and other beds. Carcharodontosaurus lived there about 100–94 million years ago, and Spinosaurus shows up in the record 100–95 million years ago. Their world bordered the Tethys Sea: a mangrove coast of vast tidal flats and winding waterways.

cret-090.title: Zealandia tears away from West Antarctica
cret-090.text: A continent most people have never heard of began breaking loose about 100 million years ago. Zealandia includes New Zealand, the Campbell Plateau, Chatham Rise, Lord Howe Rise, Norfolk Ridge and New Caledonia. Around 100 million years ago, volcanism along its margin shifted from arc magmatism, fed by a sinking plate, to rift magmatism, fed by crust pulling apart. At about the same time the Hikurangi Plateau first slid beneath New Zealand, during its collision with Gondwana. The West Antarctic Rift System began stretching in the Late Cretaceous, before the Campbell Plateau broke away. The split from West Antarctica was complete by about 84 million years ago.

cret-089.title: The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two
cret-089.text: For 34 million years, a person could have sailed from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean straight across North America. The Western Interior Seaway lasted from about 100 to 66 million years ago. It began as an Arctic arm pushing south, the Mowry Sea, which later merged with a southern embayment. The result split the continent into western and eastern landmasses, isolating their plants and animals. The seaway's bottom waters repeatedly lost their oxygen, leaving organic-rich shales that are now a major source of oil. Late in the Cretaceous the sea narrowed into an inland arm of the Gulf, and it vanished in the early Cenozoic.

cret-091.title: The long-necked giants vanish from North America
cret-091.text: Around 98 million years ago, the sauropods simply disappear from western North America. The gap that follows, lasting through most of the Late Cretaceous, is called the 'sauropod hiatus'. Proposed causes include competition with ornithischian dinosaurs, habitat lost to {{ref:cret-089}}, or gaps in sampling. Even revised dates leave a hole from the mid-Cenomanian to the mid-Campanian. The hiatus ended shortly before the Cretaceous closed, when Alamosaurus, probably an immigrant from South America, arrived. In Europe, trackways and a tooth suggest sauropods never left.

cret-093.title: The first true crocodilians
cret-093.text: Today's crocodiles, alligators and gharials belong to a lineage older than Tyrannosaurus. The first true crocodilians, the group called Crocodylia, evolved around 95 million years ago. Their ancestors had been around much longer, but this is when the line leading to every living crocodile and alligator began. That line would go on to outlast the dinosaurs around it.

cret-094.title: Lebanon's Sannine fossil beds
cret-094.text: In the hills of Lebanon, the stone splits open to reveal fish so perfect they look freshly caught. The Sannine Formation sites at Haqel, Hjoula and al-Nammoura are famous Cenomanian Lagerstätten, deposits of exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Shrimp, octopus, stingrays and bony fish are common finds. The octopuses are the true treasures, since fossil octopuses are among the rarest of all.

cret-095.title: A shallow sea splits Africa in half
cret-095.text: For a while in the Cretaceous, Africa was not one continent but two. Around 95–90 million years ago, a seaway linking the Mediterranean and the proto-Atlantic partly flooded the Tuareg Shield. A rising sea also drowned the Kem Kem world of {{ref:cret-086}}. Bivalve fossils show that a shallow sea later split Africa in half, joining the Tethys to the South Atlantic. The Benue Trough probably formed the main link to the Gulf of Guinea, through the Chad and Iullemmeden basins.

cret-092.title: The Caribbean large igneous province floods the sea floor
cret-092.text: Most of the Caribbean plate is made of lava from a single colossal outpouring. The Caribbean large igneous province holds roughly 4.4 million cubic kilometers of volcanic rock. This mass, the Caribbean–Colombian oceanic plateau, now makes up most of the plate's crust. The Galápagos hotspot began building it in the eastern Pacific about 95–90 million years ago. Volcanism spanned 139–69 million years ago but peaked between 95 and 88 million years ago. Argon–argon dating puts the main magmatism at 95–83 million years ago, with a second pulse at 81–69. A plume arriving about 86 million years ago spread eruptions into north-west South America. The main phase coincides with the oceanic anoxic event of {{ref:cret-098}}, suggesting one helped cause the other.

cret-096.title: The first mosasaurs slip into the sea
cret-096.text: The most fearsome hunters of the late Cretaceous oceans started out modestly. The first mosasaurs, marine reptiles, appear around 94 million years ago. From that start they went on to rule the Late Cretaceous seas. They filled the role left empty by the ichthyosaurs, whose decline is told in {{ref:cret-100}}.

cret-097.title: The Cenomanian–Turonian extinction
cret-097.text: For years some researchers wondered whether this extinction was real or just a trick of poor preservation. Recent work settles it: vertebrates, invertebrates and microbes truly died out at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition, about 93.9 million years ago. Planktic foraminifera, tiny shelled drifters of the open sea, vanished in five phases. The variety of burrows and tracks plummeted as the event began. It was one of the lesser extinctions tied to oceanic anoxia, when seawater runs out of oxygen, and it mostly struck marine life. Warming from the High Arctic and other large igneous provinces is thought to have driven it.

cret-098.title: OAE2: the last time the whole ocean suffocated
cret-098.text: About 93.9 million years ago, the world's oceans began to choke. The Cenomanian–Turonian oceanic anoxic event, OAE2, is considered the most recent truly global oceanic anoxic event. Sulfidic, oxygen-free water rose into the sunlit surface ocean. On the seafloor, black shale piled up, including the Livello Bonarelli at Gubbio in Italy. Osmium isotopes and trace metals point to undersea volcanism from large igneous provinces as a likely trigger. The event left a positive carbon isotope excursion, a shift in the ratio of carbon types that ranks among the Mesozoic's main carbon events. The interval had the highest carbon dioxide levels of the Cretaceous and was one of the hottest times of the Phanerozoic.

cret-099.title: The Cretaceous Thermal Maximum: a hothouse planet
cret-099.text: Crocodile-like reptiles once basked in the Canadian Arctic. Warming that began at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition peaked about 90 million years ago, in one of the hottest intervals of the Phanerozoic. Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose above 1,000 ppm, against a pre-industrial 280 ppm, and sea level stood high. Tropical seas reached at least 30 °C, perhaps 33–42 °C. The difference between equator and pole was unusually gentle. Champsosaurs lived in the Arctic, where mean yearly temperatures topped 14 °C. The warmth lasted to the Turonian–Coniacian boundary, broken only by brief cool spells. Claims of Antarctic ice during the Turonian remain disputed.

cret-100.title: Ichthyosaurs, the fish-lizards, die out
cret-100.text: Ichthyosaurs had ruled the seas since about 250 million years ago, and they did not fade slowly. Their Cretaceous variety was greater than once thought, perhaps because breaking continents lengthened the coastlines. Then the blows came. A first pulse at the start of the Cenomanian killed two of their three remaining feeding guilds, leaving only unspecialized top predators. After the anoxic event of {{ref:cret-098}}, only Platypterygius hercynicus survived, and it vanished about 93 million years ago. The end was a pair of abrupt events, probably tied to the upheaval and climate change of the Cenomanian and Turonian. Pliosaurs reportedly vanished in the same anoxic event, and {{ref:cret-096}} took over the oceans.

cret-101.title: Lava floods across Madagascar
cret-101.text: Madagascar's rocks keep a timeline of fire that runs from north to south. Flood basalts, vast sheets of runny lava, erupted across the island between about 92 and 85 million years ago, by argon–argon dating. The ages are 88–92 million years in the north and 85–88 million years in the south. The pattern suggests the eruptions swept down the island over several million years.

cret-102.title: The Andes switch from stretching to squeezing
cret-102.text: Around 90 million years ago, western South America stopped pulling apart and began to be crushed. Faster ocean spreading and stronger subduction turned the margin from extension to compression, and the Andean orogeny changed character. At about the same time, the sinking ocean floor switched from south-east to north-east motion. Back-arc basins in central Chile and Mendoza were squeezed and inverted. Uplift turned western Peru's marine basins into dry land, and erosion took hold from the Late Cretaceous onward.

cret-103.title: The earliest ticks
cret-103.text: Ticks are older than most of the animals they feed on today. The earliest examples of these small blood-sucking relatives of spiders appear around 90 million years ago. Their first hosts would have been the reptiles, birds and mammals of the Late Cretaceous world.

cret-104.title: The last carnosaurs fall
cret-104.text: One of the longest-running lines of giant predators came to an end. Carcharodontosaurids, the last definitive family of carnosaurs, became extinct in the Turonian, around 90 million years ago. Carnosaurs, a group of large meat-eating dinosaurs, had first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago. Their exit left the top-predator role to other theropods.

cret-105.title: A disputed anoxic event in the Coniacian–Santonian
cret-105.text: Not every black shale tells a global story. A minor oceanic anoxic event, recorded by organic-rich black shales, has been proposed for the Coniacian–Santonian stages, about 89.8–83.6 million years ago. Its shales are more local than those of the major Cretaceous events, found mainly in the Atlantic and nearby areas. That patchiness fuels a real disagreement: some researchers tie the shales to local conditions rather than to any global change.

cret-106.title: The Coniacian Thermal Maximum: a second peak of heat
cret-106.text: The Cretaceous hothouse had more than one summit. After {{ref:cret-099}} and a spell of slight cooling, temperatures climbed again. This second peak, the Coniacian Thermal Maximum, topped out around 87 million years ago, keeping the world in a long run of extreme warmth.

cret-107.title: The Niobrara Chalk and its flying reptiles
cret-107.text: Much of the Great Plains rests on the remains of microscopic sea life. Between 87 and 82 million years ago, the coccoliths, tiny chalky plates of microorganisms, piled up on the floor of {{ref:cret-089}} as the Niobrara Chalk. Its Smoky Hill Chalk is famous for marine fossils: plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, pterosaurs and primitive aquatic birds. The pterosaur Pteranodon, with wingspans over 6 m, turns up in most of its layers. About 1,200 Pteranodon specimens are known.

cret-108.title: Maiasaura, the good mother lizard
cret-108.text: The first proof that dinosaurs cared for their young came from a nesting ground in Montana. Maiasaura, a duck-billed dinosaur, lived in Montana and Alberta about 86.3 to 70.6 million years ago. It nested in colonies of closely packed earthen mounds, about 7 m apart, each holding 30 to 40 eggs. Hatchlings had weak legs but worn teeth. They could not have walked off to feed, so adults must have brought food to the nest.

cret-109.title: The first duck-billed hadrosaurids
cret-109.text: The duck-billed dinosaurs would become some of the most common plant-eaters of the latest Cretaceous. Their family, the hadrosaurids, first appears around 86 million years ago. Its members included nest-builders like {{ref:cret-108}}.

cret-111.title: The Praia Grande crater, hidden off Brazil
cret-111.text: Off the coast of Brazil, a scar from space lies under 4 km of rock. An impact in the Santonian made the Praia Grande crater, about 20 km across, in the Santos Basin. Buried deep beneath younger sediment, the crater is well preserved, shielded from the erosion that wipes out most impact scars.

cret-112.title: The long Late Cretaceous cooling begins
cret-112.text: From the Santonian on, the great Cretaceous hothouse began to lose its heat. Global climate started to cool near the end of the mid-Cretaceous warmth, a trend that ran on through the Campanian. Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera shells record peak warmth in the Turonian, then gradual surface cooling to the end of the Maastrichtian. Tropical sea surfaces fell from about 35 °C in the early Campanian to about 28 °C in the Maastrichtian. Turtles declined during one Campanian cool spell. The Late Cretaceous stayed warmer than today, but its cooling trend carried on into the Cenozoic. Whether continental ice sheets formed is unclear, because ocean-temperature estimates conflict.

openers.late-cretaceous-epoch: The Late Cretaceous began in a hothouse and ended in catastrophe. For 34 million years a shallow sea split North America in two, while giant spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids ruled the tidal flats of North Africa. In the oceans, marine reptiles perfected the art of crushing shells. On land and in the air, the ancestors of modern birds and the first true crocodilians appeared, both lineages that would outlast the dinosaurs. Meanwhile Zealandia began to tear away from Antarctica, part of a long breakup that would reshape the southern continents.

cret-097.text: Tiny single-celled organisms with shells that drift in the open sea.

cret-101.text: A vast sheet of runny basalt lava that erupts and spreads over a huge area.
